title: Effects of temporarily induced ametropia on upper body posture and postural control
summary:
The planned study analyzes the effects of short-term induced ametropia on posture and balance regulation. 
To date, too little is known about whether and to what extent eye diseases can also lead to postural abnormalities, which in turn could end in back problems. Therefore, the present study should help to better understand the interaction between vision and posture, since various eye diseases are associated with the loss of vision in only one eye and the monovision often used to correct presbyopia, i.e., adjusting one eye for near (+1.5) and leaving the other eye for distance, could lead to postural abnormalities and thus also contribute to the "common complaint" of back pain.

interventions.name: A total of 49 healthy adults between 18 and 75 years of age will be examined for the influence of seven different visual conditions (open eyes, closed eyes, +12.0 dpt on both eyes,+12 dpt dominant eye,+12 dpt nondominant eye,+1.5 dpt dominant eye,+ 1.5 dpt nondominant eye) on upper body posture and

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Patients between 18 and 75 years
Exclusion criteria:
- Patients with a visible or known scoliosis (COBB angle >10°).
- Patients with stiffening operations on the spine, hip, knee or ankle joint
- Patients with intervertebral disc replacement
- Patients with monocular or binocular visual loss (visual acuity less than 0.8)
- Patients with non-intact stereo vision (disparity over 550 arcseconds) (tested with Lang test)
